learning_goal: Recognise a typical vertebra from any angle, and say which part bears weight, which encloses the cord, and how a cervical, thoracic and lumbar vertebra differ.

structures.name: second lumbar vertebra
structures.label: L2 — the exemplar
structures.narration: A lumbar vertebra shows every feature of the typical plan at its largest: a big body in front, an arch behind, and processes off the arch.

structures.label: Vertebral body
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: measured on the L2 mesh by tools/derive-vertebra-landmarks.mjs — midline ray: solid from Y -114.7 to -81.5 — 33.2 mm of bone in front of the canal; centred vertically in a 24.6 mm span of body · snapped 12.5 mm onto the parent's surface (-y, the aspect the narration describes): the measured point marks a volume, and a patch can only be painted on a surface
structures.narration: The weight-bearing block in front. It gets bigger as you go down the column, because each one carries everything above it.

structures.label: Vertebral foramen
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: measured on the L2 mesh by tools/derive-vertebra-landmarks.mjs — midline ray: hollow from Y -81.5 to -63.8 — a 17.7 mm gap between body and arch · snapped 8.4 mm onto the parent's surface: the measured point marks a volume, and a patch can only be painted on a surface
structures.narration: The hole between the body and the arch. Stack them and they form the vertebral canal that carries the cord.

structures.label: Spinous process
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: measured on the L2 mesh by tools/derive-vertebra-landmarks.mjs — most posterior bone within 5 mm of the midline: Y -34.0, at Z 1007.8 — -19.8 mm from mid-height (63 vertices at the tip)
structures.narration: The blade pointing straight back. This is the bump you feel down someone’s back, and on a lumbar vertebra it is short, flat and blunt.

structures.label: Transverse process (left)
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: measured on the L2 mesh by tools/derive-vertebra-landmarks.mjs — widest bone to the left: X 37.5 mm (+X is the body's left; 52 vertices within 3 mm of the tip)
structures.narration: The wing pointing sideways. It is a lever for muscles, and in the thorax it carries a facet for the rib.

structures.label: Transverse process (right)
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: measured on the L2 mesh by tools/derive-vertebra-landmarks.mjs — widest bone to the right: X -41.2 mm (51 vertices within 3 mm of the tip)
structures.narration: The wing pointing sideways on the other side.

structures.label: Superior articular process (left)
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: measured on the L2 mesh by tools/derive-vertebra-landmarks.mjs — highest bone behind the canal on that side: Z 1051.1, 23.6 mm above mid-height
structures.narration: Points upwards to grip the vertebra above. These small synovial joints are what let the column move.

structures.label: Inferior articular process (left)
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: measured on the L2 mesh by tools/derive-vertebra-landmarks.mjs — lowest bone behind the canal on that side: Z 1003.8, 23.8 mm below mid-height
structures.narration: Points downwards to grip the vertebra below. Together with the disc, these are the three joints between any two vertebrae.

structures.label: Superior articular process (right)
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: measured on the L2 mesh by tools/derive-vertebra-landmarks.mjs — highest bone behind the canal on that side: Z 1050.3, 22.8 mm above mid-height
structures.narration: The upward-facing joint surface on the other side.

structures.label: Inferior articular process (right)
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: measured on the L2 mesh by tools/derive-vertebra-landmarks.mjs — lowest bone behind the canal on that side: Z 1004.2, 23.4 mm below mid-height
structures.narration: The downward-facing joint surface on the other side.

structures.label: Pedicle (left)
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: measured on the L2 mesh by tools/derive-vertebra-landmarks.mjs — lateral ray at Y -79.5 splits into two masses; the left one runs X 6.7 to 15.5 — 8.8 mm thick (run of 5 slices)
structures.narration: The short thick bridge from the body back to the arch. Its own lower notch, meeting the upper notch of the pedicle below, makes the intervertebral foramen where the nerve leaves.

structures.label: Pedicle (right)
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: measured on the L2 mesh by tools/derive-vertebra-landmarks.mjs — lateral ray at Y -79.5 splits into two masses; the right one runs X -15.1 to -6.1 — 9.1 mm thick (run of 5 slices)
structures.narration: The bridge on the other side. The two pedicles are the walls of the canal.

structures.label: Lamina (left)
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: measured on the L2 mesh by tools/derive-vertebra-landmarks.mjs — lateral ray at Y -65.5 splits into two masses; the left one runs X 4.2 to 13.9 — 9.7 mm thick (run of 7 slices)
structures.narration: The flat plate running back from the pedicle to the spinous process. This is the bone removed in a laminectomy.

structures.label: Lamina (right)
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: measured on the L2 mesh by tools/derive-vertebra-landmarks.mjs — lateral ray at Y -65.5 splits into two masses; the right one runs X -15.7 to -4.1 — 11.5 mm thick (run of 7 slices)
structures.narration: The plate on the other side. The two laminae meet in the midline and form the roof of the canal.

structures.name: sixth thoracic vertebra
structures.label: T6 — thoracic
structures.narration: The same plan with costal facets added for the ribs, a heart-shaped body, and a long spine sloping downwards.

structures.name: fifth cervical vertebra
structures.label: C5 — cervical
structures.narration: The same plan shrunk: small body, large triangular foramen, a hole in each transverse process, and a bifid spine.

structures.name: first lumbar vertebra
structures.label: L1 — above
structures.narration: The vertebra above — its inferior articular processes grip L2.

structures.name: third lumbar vertebra
structures.label: L3 — below
structures.narration: The vertebra below — L2 grips it in turn, and the pair leave a gap for the nerve root.

structures.name: intervertebral disk of first lumbar vertebra
structures.label: Disc above L2
structures.narration: The pad between L1 and L2 — the joint between the two bodies.

structures.name: intervertebral disk of second lumbar vertebra
structures.label: Disc below L2
structures.narration: The pad between L2 and L3.

views.title: One unit of the column
views.narration: Every vertebra is built to the same plan. Take one out of the stack and the plan is easy to read.

views.title: The plan from above
views.narration: From above: the thick body sits in front, the arch sweeps back from it, and the ring between them is the vertebral foramen. The blunt process pointing straight back is the spinous process; the two pointing sideways are the transverse processes.

views.title: Name the parts
views.narration: Now put the names on. Body in front, then a pedicle on each side, then a lamina on each side meeting behind at the spinous process. That ring of body, pedicles and laminae is the vertebral foramen. Off the arch come the transverse processes sideways and the articular processes up and down.

views.title: Body in front, ring behind
views.narration: Cut across it and the two jobs separate cleanly. Solid bone in front takes the weight; the hollow ring behind protects the cord. Stack the rings and you have the vertebral canal.

views.title: How the neighbours lock on
views.narration: Two vertebrae meet in three places: a disc between the bodies and a small synovial joint on each side between the articular processes. Their pedicles leave a window between them — the notch under the pedicle above meeting the notch over the pedicle below — and that window is the intervertebral foramen, through which the spinal nerve leaves.

views.title: Same plan, three regions
views.narration: Put the three side by side and each region announces itself. A hole in the transverse process means cervical. A facet for a rib means thoracic. A large kidney-shaped body with a flat blunt spine means lumbar.

gaps: The named parts of a typical vertebra have no separate models in the catalog — a whole vertebra is the smallest unit it holds. They are therefore placed as landmark anchors on the L2 mesh, measured on the geometry by tools/derive-vertebra-landmarks.mjs rather than estimated.

Each anchor is status "needs-review": every one was verified to sit where its name says (solid bone for the body, pedicles and laminae; open space for the vertebral foramen; on the surface for the processes), but no human has signed them off yet.
The regional features that make T6 and C5 atypical — the costal facets and the foramen transversarium — are still narrated rather than labelled. They need the same treatment on their own meshes.
